extracted_by: hand, T-0335 — the Democrat read, August 1835
note: Vol. II No. 18. THE RICHEST OF THE FOUR, and the issue this ticket takes the TOWN ORDINANCES from: page 1 columns 1 and 2 carry the Trustees' by-laws, passed 5 August 1835 over Hugunin's and Alex. N. Fullerton's names, and this printing sets them line by line where 12 August weaves them into two 5,000-character segmenter columns and 26 August carries only the tail. Six claims (c001-c006) hold them, and three passages in them are directly modellable: the half-sidewalk-and-two-months rule for a building site, the five-dollar penalty for riding across a bridge walk, and section 18's eighteen inches of stove pipe above every roof. Section 22's hay-stacking limit walks a six-vertex boundary through named streets and is the only documented statement in this corpus of where the built town was held to end in the scene year. Page 3 carries the month's best-placed shop (Sarah D. Howe's room in the house Dr. Austin occupies), the only numbered street address in the month (No. 1 South Water Street, near the Draw Bridge) and twenty-one named lots offered to lease. STANDING ADVERTISEMENTS unchanged from 5 August are not re-claimed here. THE LETTER LIST is the same 31 July list, printed a third time; signature claimed, names deferred to T-0336. NOT CLAIMED, AND DELIBERATELY: the 'DESTRUCTIVE FIRE' on page 3 column 1, which consumes a book store, Strickland & Gaylord's store, law offices, a looking-glass and comb factory and a coffee house for $55,000. It stands immediately under a 'Cleveland Whig, July 30' credit, the words 'of Cleveland' survive inside it, its named sufferers are not Chicago names, and no source records a fire of that size in Chicago in 1835 — it is read as an out-of-town reprint and is NOT claimed as this town's, on the same principle that quarantined the out-of-county estray notices in Vol. I No. 1. Also not claimed: pages 1-2 national politics and the Ottawa probate notices.

claims.normalized: [The Trustees of the Town of Chicago do] [en]act [the] […] following [Laws] and Ordinances of said town: [any person] who shall be guilty of any of [the acts here]inafter [mentioned] shall be [punished as herea]fter prescribed. […] [No p]erson shal[l] place or cause to [be placed any bric]k, ston[e], timber, lumber [or ot]her m[a]terials for [building on any] street, side walk, al[ley … or on any vacant ground …] without permission from the Pre[sident or the] Trustees, under the penalty [of … dollars] for every off[e]nce, and the fur[ther penalt]y of five dollars for each and every [twenty-four] hours during which the articles or [lumber] shall re[m]ain [in] any such [street, alley, square] or other vacant [ground …] [and it shall be the duty of the] [cons]table to re[move] the same, provided that it shall be law[ful for any] person engaged in the erection of [any build]ings upon any lot to d[eposit] […] his so t[a]k[in]g o[f m]aterials […] upon the street […] [ad]joining, pro[vided not m]ore than one ha[l]f [o]f the side walk […] of the ca[rri]ag[e] wa[y] of the street [next to the building] erecting shall be obstructed, [and] for [no] longer time [than] two months, with[out] […] permission […] No person shall place, deposit or [leave] any [c]ask, bo[x]es or crates, goods or [other articles] for sale or other purpose, [upon the] side walk in front of any store or [other building] farther than four feet into the [same …] [without] express permission from one of the [T]rustees, under the penalty of two dollars for [ea]ch, and [a] like penalty for every twen[ty-four hours af]ter [n]o[tice] such obstruction shall remain […]
claims.notes: THE TOWN GOVERNS ITS OWN STREET WIDTH, AND THE NUMBERS ARE MODELLABLE. Three of them: building materials may not be left in a street at all without leave; a builder MAY occupy the street beside his own lot, but not more than one half of the sidewalk nor of the carriage way, and for no longer than two months; and goods may stand on the sidewalk in front of a store no farther than four feet into it. That is a rule for what a Chicago street looked like in August 1835 — timber and brick piled against half a footway, boxes standing four feet out from a shop front, and both of them ordinary enough to be legislated for. The column is the worst-cut matter this ticket claims, two physical columns woven line by line, so almost every clause carries a supply; the sections are numbered in the printed ordinance and the numbers are among the things the column lost. The 12 August issue prints the same forme in a shape a quote cannot be built from at all.

claims.notes: THE BRIDGES GET AN ORDINANCE OF THEIR OWN, AND IT IS A SENTENCE THIS RECONSTRUCTION CAN BUILD FROM: nobody may RIDE or DRIVE across the walk of a Chicago bridge — he dismounts and walks, on pain of five dollars, five times the penalty for riding along an ordinary sidewalk. A bridge with a walk on it that a horse is kept off is a bridge with a distinguishable footway, and it is the only statement in the corpus so far about how the town's bridges were used rather than where they stood. The section numbers are cut away and are not supplied; the penalty figures survive. Cross walks, pavements and sewers are all named as things the town maintained and could be fined for damaging.

claims.normalized: [No] person shall keep a Billiard [Table, Faro] Bank or any other instrument or [device for gaming …] where or [with which] […] [under a penal]ty of twenty five dollars […] for [ea]ch […] offence […] [twenty-four] hours during which […] [he] shall continue to keep the same […] [No person shall throw or deposit any dead animal,] p[u]tr[i]d meat or fish [or …] veg[e]t[a]bles or any other of[fensive substance … in]to the Chicago River or [upon the banks thereof]; and any person [who shall vi]ol[a]te the provisions of this section [shall remove the same] and pay the pen[alty …] [The owner] or occupant of any [lot in said town shall not suffer any dead animal] […] to be or remain in or upon [the same, or in the alley or street between the same and] the street or alley adjoining, [under a penalty of not more than five dollars] […] [and if such animal] shall be or remain (after n[otice]) […] of the same, [up]on [any] lot or [ten]ement, […] the President and each of [the Trustees of said town are] authorized […] [as] often as it shall [come to their] knowledge that any nuisance [exists] […]
claims.notes: THE RIVER IS PROTECTED BY NAME, AND SO ARE THE ALLEYS BEHIND THE LOTS. Nothing dead may be thrown into the Chicago River; nothing dead may be left lying on a lot or in the alley between a lot and its street; the President and each Trustee may abate a nuisance the moment they hear of one. Read together with the fire wardens' house-by-house inspection (claim c006), it is a picture of a town of some three thousand that had already worked out it must police what its own back lots held. A billiard table or faro bank carries the heaviest penalty in the whole ordinance, twenty-five dollars — five times a fire offence. The column is shredded and the section numbers are gone; every supply is bracketed and the offensive-substance list is read against the 26 August printing of the same passage.

Sec. [20]. No person shall fire any squib, [cr]acker, gun-powder or firework, or fire any [gun] or pistol in said town unless by permission of one of the trustees, under a pen[al]ty of two dollars.
claims.notes: THE STOVE-PIPE ORDINANCE, AND IT IS THE ONE PASSAGE IN THIS MONTH THAT DICTATES ROOF GEOMETRY. Section 18 says, in August 1835 and under a five-dollar penalty, that every stove pipe or chimney passing through a roof SHALL BE CARRIED AT LEAST EIGHTEEN INCHES ABOVE IT; that no stove pipe may go out through a side or end wall at all; and that where a pipe passes a wooden or lath-and-plaster partition it must be sleeved in a stone or earthen cylinder, surrounded by brick, or run through a tin or sheet-iron plate held a quarter inch clear, with three inches clear of any woodwork. A roof line in this reconstruction that carries stub pipes, or pipes out through a gable end, is contradicted by the town's own by-law. Sections 15 to 17 are the same fear from the other side: shavings swept out of a shop once a week, no bonfires in a street or on a lot without leave. The long clause from 'an inch of the pipe' to 'shall be passed' is read whole from the 12 August printing of the identical forme, where this printing's column runs the two halves of the sentence into one line; it is bracketed as a supply here because THIS column does not carry it.

claims.notes: A HAY-STACKING BOUNDARY WALKED STREET BY STREET, AND IT IS A POLYGON. Washington street at the United States Reservation, west to Canal Street, north to Kinzie Street, east to Wolcott street, thence to Illinois Street, and thence to Lake Michigan — six vertices, all of them named streets this reconstruction already carries, describing the ground the Trustees thought dense enough that a hay stack in it was a fire risk. It is the only documented statement in the corpus of where the BUILT town was held to end in the scene year, and it is drawn from the fort's reservation round the forks and back to the lake. Section 21 is its companion: a fire warden per district walking into every house, store and shop nine months of the year, checking the chimneys, ovens, stoves, pipes, hearths, boilers and wash houses that section 18 regulates. Passed 5 August 1835 over the names of the President, Hugunin, and the Secretary, Alexander N. Fullerton. The section 22 preamble is read from the 12 and 26 August printings, which set it whole where this column jumps from 'unsafe' to 'North to the intersection'.

That is rare in this corpus: nearly every anchor the papers give is a store, an office or a public house, and this one is a dwelling. The date is Saturday 22 August 1835, three days after the paper. A 'Juvenile Society' selling children's work by subscription is the town's second charitable institution to appear in the corpus. The placement is street-only on Water street — the house is named but nothing sets it against a neighbour.

claims.normalized: To the Ministers and Members of the Baptist denomination in the Northern part of [Illinois], [the] North-Western parts of Indiana and the Territory of [W]isconsin: [it is] proposed to conv[e]ne a meeting of Mini[s]ters and Delegates from Baptist chur[c]hes at D[u] Page, Cook co., Ill., on Tuesday the [15]th day of September at 10 o'clock, for the purpose of forming an association within the limits above mentioned […] Communications on this subject are requested, for the present, to be addressed to either of the undersigned, who are pastors of Baptist churches, at the r[espective] places of the[ir] residence. ISAAC T. HINTON, Chicago; J. E. AMBROSE, Plainfield; A. B. HUBBARD, Du Page. August 18, 1835.
claims.notes: THE BAPTIST PASTOR OF CHICAGO IS NAMED, AND HE IS ONE OF THREE IN A REGION THE SIZE OF A STATE. Isaac T. Hinton signs for Chicago, Ambrose for Plainfield, Hubbard for Du Page — three settled Baptist churches between Lake Michigan and the Territory of Wisconsin, meeting at Du Page in September to make an association. For a reconstruction that must decide which denominations had a building in Chicago in 1835 this is direct evidence that the Baptists had a pastor here; it says nothing about what he preached in. The Methodist chapel and the Presbyterian church are both named elsewhere in this corpus as meeting places; no Baptist meeting house is.

claims.notes: TEN ARRIVALS IN NINE DAYS, AND THE HARBOUR THEY CAME INTO IS DESCRIBED IN THE SAME MONTH'S SOUNDINGS. Grand River, St. Joseph, Milwaukee, Oswego, Detroit and Buffalo — the lake trade Chicago lived on, at a rate of better than one vessel a day, each with its master named. Two of them, the Indiana and the Llewellyn, are back inside a week, which is what a St. Joseph or Grand River run looked like. The 5 August issue carries Lieut. Brown's soundings of the same harbour: thirteen feet between the piers where the channel is six hundred feet wide, twenty where it is four hundred, and nowhere in the channel less than ten. A vessel list is therefore not decoration here — it is the traffic those piers were built to take.

claims.notes: TWENTY-ONE NAMED LOTS AND A WHOLE BLOCK, OFFERED TO LEASE ON STREETS THIS RECONSTRUCTION ALREADY CARRIES. Block and lot numbers on Lake street, North Water street, Kinzie street, Canal and Clinton streets, and Block 15 entire on North Water — a document that says which ground in the platted town was still UNBUILT and available in August 1835, which is exactly the kind of negative evidence a reconstruction of a half-empty town needs and rarely gets. An agent leasing rather than selling is worth noticing in the middle of the speculative summer. The lots pair with their streets down a two-column bracket in the original setting and the pairing is read off the printed brackets; each supplied 'block' and street attribution is bracketed. The 12 August printing of the same advertisement, dated 8 August, sets the first line without the '40 feet of Lot 7 in block 18' and is the reason the reading is taken from here.

TH[E] subscriber having taken a shop on Dea[r]born street nearly opposite the Eagle Coffee House, where he intends to carry on the business in all its various and most complicated branches, and hopes by strict attention and promptness of execution to merit a share of public patronage. GEORGE [H]OLSMAN. August 10, 1835.
claims.notes: THE SAME SHOP, IN THE SAME ELEVEN WORDS, TAKEN BY A DIFFERENT TAILOR THREE WEEKS LATER. Cooley and Hol[b]man announced on 22 July that they had taken 'a shop, on Dearborn Street, nearly opposite the Eagle Coffee House' (chicago_democrat_1835_08_05.json c005); George Holsman announces on 10 August that he has taken a shop on Dearborn street nearly opposite the Eagle Coffee House. Either a two-man partnership became one man inside three weeks, or two tailors' shops stood within a few doors of each other opposite the same coffee house. The papers of August do not decide it and neither does this claim; the two names are NOT merged, because same surname with a different spelling is exactly the judgement identity.json exists to make explicitly. What the pair does establish beyond doubt is a tailoring frontage on Dearborn street opposite the Eagle Coffee House, continuously advertised through the month.

claims.notes: THE MONTH'S BEST-PLACED SHOP, AND IT IS A WOMAN'S. A room in Lake-street, in the house occupied by Dr. Austin, opposite Dr. Temple's — two anchors on one line, both of them men who advertise in the same paper, and Austin's own advertisement in the 12 August issue puts his office 'on Lake street, near the post office' (chicago_democrat_1835_08_12.json c004). So one Lake Street house holds a physician's office and a dressmaker's room, faces a second physician's, and stands near the post office: four uses within a few doors, from three independent notices. She is also hiring four apprentices, which makes it a workroom and not a parlour. A 'Sarah D. Howe' stands on the post-office letter list printed in this same issue, the strongest corroboration a listed name can get, and T-0336 will meet her there.

claims.notes: THE DENTIST BECOMES A DOCTOR TOO, IN THE SAME ROOM. On 5 August Kennicott advertised as SURGEON DENTIST only, from an office opposite the Exchange on Lake-street, with a year's practice behind him; on 19 August the same office offers 'both … Medicine and Dentistry' over a copy date of that very day. A practice widening inside three weeks is the kind of change that dates a fitting-out, and the address does not move. That makes four separate medical men advertising in Chicago in one month — Kennicott, Austin, the Dr. Temple whose house Sarah Howe faces, and the Dr. A. H. Howland of the letter list — three of them on Lake Street.

claims.notes: A NUMBERED ADDRESS AND A BRIDGE IN ONE LINE — the only street NUMBER any Chicago advertisement in this month carries, and the only building the corpus places against the draw bridge. No. 1 South Water Street, near the Draw Bridge, opening on the first of September 1835: a stock not yet landed, on premises already taken, five days before the Democrat's run ends. The draw bridge is the Dearborn Street bridge over the main river, and the town's own ordinance of 5 August forbids riding or driving on a bridge walk (claim c002), so this is a grocery placed at the busiest crossing the town had. Merchants, tavern keepers and manufacturers are addressed as distinct trades, and families are supplied separately — a wholesale house that also served the street it stood on.

claims.notes: A SEVENTH ATTORNEY, AND THE ONLY ONE ON LAKE STREET. The 5 August cards put Curtiss on South Water, Collins and Abell on Dearborn, Moore in Kinzie's new store and Spring beside the Tremont; Caton's is new in this issue and it is 'one door west of' a building whose name the column cut away with the next line. The offset text is kept verbatim precisely because the anchor is missing: a placement that names a direction and a distance but not the thing it measures from cannot place anything, and the class is therefore relative with the anchor recorded as unreadable rather than guessed at. John Dean Caton later sat on the Illinois Supreme Court; in August 1835 he is a young man advertising a room.
